member.name: T:AshForge.ModLoader.AppearanceRepair
member.summary:
Makes a save that our own dec-cache bug already corrupted LOADABLE again.
stops us writing any more of them. This repairs the ones already on disk.
── WHAT IS WRONG WITH THOSE SAVES ───────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────── A pawn was handed a HairStyleDec from a discarded parse generation, so the writer refused it and wrote "<name>_DELETED". On load, dec cannot resolve that name and — with no error, because a missing dec resolves to an empty string and then to null — hands the pawn a NULL HairStyle. The first time the map tries to draw that pawn, `RigController.UpdateAppearance` dereferences it, NREs, and `Map.Activate` never finishes: the map stays inactive forever and the log fills with thousands of "tried to update an inactive map".
── THE REPAIR ───────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────── Give the pawn a real hairstyle before the renderer touches it. `AppearanceData` is a CLASS, so the pawn keeps the repair: the next save writes a valid name and the save heals itself permanently.
★ This is deliberately a REPAIR, not a workaround: it does not paper over a live bug, because after DecCacheGuard no correctly-loaded pawn can reach here with a null hairstyle. If this ever fires on a save made AFTER the guard shipped, that is a real signal — so it says so, loudly, once.

member.name: T:AshForge.ModLoader.Contracts.BrokerContracts
member.summary:
Typed contract stubs for every published ashforge.* capability (broker spec §10.2).
WHY THIS EXISTS. Without it, a third-party author writes ctx.Query<ColonyNetWorth>(new CapabilityId( "ashforge", "colony.net_worth", 1)) — three facts (id, version, payload type) they have to get right from documentation, with a runtime type-guard rejection as the only feedback. Each stub below binds those three together in one place, so the compiler enforces what the broker would otherwise only reject at runtime. It is the difference between guessing at a channel and programming against a documented API.
★ THE STUBS DELIBERATELY DO NOT REDECLARE THE PAYLOAD TYPES. They reference the loader's ( et al). A copied payload type would be a DIFFERENT CLR Type in the mod's assembly, and the broker's runtime type guard compares against the contract's PayloadType — so every query would fall back to the default and every provider registration would be rejected. Same reason the Mod Kit ships these as a thin facade over AshLoader.dll, never as a standalone copy of the contracts.
★ Deriving a provider from ProviderBase makes BRK003 (declared version ≠ payload type) UNREPRESENTABLE: the capability id is supplied by the base, and the payload type is fixed by the generic. You choose only a priority (see the priority bands in HANDOFF_BROKER.md) and the pure read.
Every stub is a pure convenience wrapper — the underlying surface stays open for anyone who needs it. Adding a capability to without adding a stub here is caught by the "contract stub coverage" test in tools/BrokerTests.

member.name: T:AshForge.ModLoader.BrokerSaveDiagnostics
member.summary:
Save diagnostics (Resolution Panel spec §7, broker spec §9): remember WHICH PROVIDERS were bound to which capabilities when a save was written, and on load raise a non-blocking notice for any that changed.
"This save was created with Wealth & Trade providing colony net worth. It is now provided by Deep Economy Overhaul. Economy-derived values (raid scaling, prices) may differ."
INFORMATIONAL ONLY. It never gates loading — that would break save portability, which is the whole point of the standalone-first invariant. A save made with a provider installed must still load without it (resolving to the loader default), and vice versa.
★ WE RECORD BINDINGS, NOT VALUES. At load time nothing has been queried yet, so there is no provenance to compare against — but every provider has already registered (mod `Init` runs long before the sidecar is dispatched on `World.ActivateMap`). So the comparable, stable fact is "which provider WOULD win", computed the same way resolution computes it: effective priority desc, load order asc, skipping user-disabled and circuit-broken providers, falling through to the floor.
★ REGISTERED UNDER ITS OWN MOD ID, not . Fault counts are cumulative per id, and the core id is the capability default floor's id — pouring this diagnostic's faults into that bucket would muddy the floor's fault log (and, before the floor was made un-disableable, could have taken it down). This id is ordinary: if these callbacks ever throw repeatedly, the circuit breaker disables the diagnostics — which is exactly the right blast radius for a purely informational feature.

member.name: T:AshForge.ModLoader.Bus
member.summary:
The AshForge event bus — CORE (lives in the loader, not a mod), so it exists before anything subscribes. Mods publish and subscribe by name and never touch Harmony; AshForge owns the emit points (the Harmony postfixes that feed game events in) and the catalog of event names/payloads (see ).

Isolation is not optional: a subscriber that throws is caught and attributed to its owning mod via , a mod auto-disabled by the fault policy stops receiving events, and one bad subscriber never breaks the publisher or its fellow subscribers.

── THE BUG THIS EXISTS TO KILL (proven 2026-07-13) ──────────────────────────────────────────────────────── `Dec.Database.Clear()` clears the database and nulls the fields of [StaticReferences] classes. It knows nothing about caches the GAME keeps on its own types. And the game keeps one:
class HairStyleDec : Dec { public static readonly List<HairStyleDec> AllMaleStyles = new(); public static readonly List<HairStyleDec> AllFemaleStyles = new(); public override void PostLoad(...) { ... AllMaleStyles.Add(this); ... } // ← APPENDS }
Every `ParserModular.Finish()` runs `PostLoad` on every dec, so every parse APPENDS a whole fresh generation of HairStyleDecs on top of the last one — while only the FINAL generation is registered in the database. New pawns pick their hair from that LIST, not from the database:
HairStyle = (Gender == Female ? AllFemaleStyles : AllMaleStyles).PickRandomElement()
…so a pawn can be handed an instance the save writer will refuse: `WriteDec` compares by REFERENCE against the database and, on a mismatch, writes "<name>_DELETED" — which reads back as a silent NULL and NREs in `RigController.UpdateAppearance` during `Map.Activate`. The map never activates. The save is dead.
We parse more than once whenever a mod fails def validation (the bisect path in ). MEASURED: with one bad mod present, 6 parses → the lists held 6 copies of every style → 6 of 7 pawns were unsaveable. With no bad mod: 1 parse, 0 duplicates, every pawn saved cleanly.
── WHY BASELINE-RESTORE AND NOT JUST Clear() ────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────── Clearing is only CORRECT for caches that `PostLoad` REPOPULATES. Reflection cannot distinguish those from a cache populated ONCE (a static initializer or a lazy snapshot of the database — the game already has one of those shape: `PlantDec[] AllCrops = Database<PlantDec>.List.Where(x => x.IsCrop)`). Blanket-clearing such a cache would empty it with nothing to refill it — a quieter, worse bug than the one we are fixing, shipped by the very code meant to prevent it.
So: snapshot each cache's PRISTINE contents once, before our first parse, and RESTORE to that baseline before each subsequent one. • append-on-PostLoad cache → baseline is empty → restore == clear → PostLoad refills it. ✔ • populated-once cache → baseline holds its contents → preserved. ✔ • a parse that THROWS → the caches are still restorable, not left empty. ✔ The right behaviour falls out of the baseline; we never have to guess which kind a cache is.

member.name: T:AshForge.ModLoader.ModFault
member.summary:
The single, invocation-agnostic mod-fault policy for the whole loader.
This is deliberately NOT tied to how mod code was reached (a Harmony patch, a bus subscriber, a lifecycle hook, a scheduled tick, …). It only knows: a fault was attributed to mod X — log it, count it, disable X past a threshold, and expose the disabled-set. Every execution surface in AshForge routes its faults here so attribution and the disabled-state stay single-sourced (two half-overlapping isolation systems would let a mod disabled on one path keep firing on another — invisible at 5 mods, a support nightmare at 500).
THE INVARIANT (document it loudly, never route around it): no subsystem in AshForge ever calls mod code directly — only ever through . Each new surface that obeys this inherits isolation / attribution / disable-respect by construction, and isolation code is never written again.

So without this exemption, five cumulative loader-side faults — across ANY capability's default/validate/scalar/compose — would auto-disable "ashforge.loader", after which every capability's default floor silently stops running and yields default(T) (i.e. null for the reference payloads). That would break the broker's load-bearing "a Query NEVER fails" invariant, silently, forever, with no provider at fault. The floor is not a mod: it is the guarantee everything else falls back to. Faults here are still counted and LOGGED loudly — they just never gate the floor.

member.name: T:AshForge.ModLoader.ModSaveData
member.summary:
Mod save-data attachment — a standard way for a mod to attach its own blob to the game's save and get it back on load, with a version for migration. The persistence dependency every *stateful* mod needs (the World Map's node state is its first consumer); built before that mod, not before all mods.
DESIGN — sidecar, not injection. AoA saves are a single dec-Recorder XML document written by the game. AshForge does NOT splice mod data into that document (that would couple every mod to dec's format and risk corrupting the base save). Instead each save file user://saves/<name>.xml gets a parallel sidecar <name>.xml.ashforge holding all mods' blobs. The sidecar is independent: it can't break the game save, it survives game updates, and a missing/corrupt sidecar just means mods load with no prior state.
LIFECYCLE (driven by ): save → (postfix SaveMenu.StartSaveToFile) load → (postfix SaveMenu.StartLoadFromFile — read sidecar off disk) → (postfix World.ActivateMap — hand each mod its blob exactly when the loaded world goes live, so a handler may touch World.Active)
Every provider callback runs through (THE INVARIANT) — a mod that throws while saving or loading is isolated and attributed, and never breaks the save, the load, or another mod's data.

If we parse once to *validate* and then throw that away and parse again to *load*, a game cache can be left holding instances from the discarded parse while the live database owns different ones — and dec serialises a reference whose object ≠ the database's as <name>_DELETED, so a game saved that session won't re-load (it crashes restoring the missing dec). Only if the combined load actually errors do we bisect individual mods (which re-parses); that path is rare (a genuinely broken mod) and self-heals next launch once the validation cache makes the load a single clean parse.

Loader-drawn and mod-drawn are equally defeatable AFTER load. That is not the difference that matters. • The difference is BEFORE load. A mod-drawn indicator is removable with a checkbox — the same Mod Manager the player is already in. The attack is then one extra sentence of social engineering ("and turn off the AshForge status mod"), which needs no malware and leaves no trace. Drawing it in the loader forces an attacker into active tamper, which is unambiguous malice and leaves evidence.
So the rule is narrowed rather than discarded: a mod draws FEATURES; the loader draws the one control whose whole value is that the thing it warns about cannot switch it off.

Four test projects consume AshLoader through a ProjectReference, and the mod csprojs show the Linux build resolves the game via $(GameData); a hardcoded GodotSharp HintPath here would flow into all of them and break the Linux loader build. This is also just the loader's existing idiom: it never compile-references dec or the game assembly either. member.name: T:AshForge.ModLoader.WorldStateBroker
member.summary:
The AshForge World-State Broker — CORE (lives in the loader, like ), so official capabilities exist before any mod registers a provider. It is the sibling of the event bus: the bus carries "things that happened" (fire-and-forget); the broker answers "what is true right now" (a query arbitrated to one value). See LOADER-BROKER-001.
THE LOAD-BEARING INVARIANT — standalone is the floor: every registered capability has a loader Default at priority 0, so ALWAYS returns a valid value even with zero providers installed. Installing more mods upgrades signal quality; it never gates function. A missing or throwing provider degrades to the default, never to a crash.
Every crossing into mod code (a provider's Provide, an aggregate Compose supplied by a mod, an OnChanged handler) runs through — inheriting isolation, fault attribution, and the auto-disable circuit breaker for free (the loader's one-chokepoint invariant). The broker persists NO gameplay state: providers own and persist their own data, so saves stay portable across changes to the installed mod set.

★★ DELIBERATELY internal. A mod assembly cannot see it, so a mod cannot swap in an authority that says yes to itself — which would make the whole gate decorative. The test harnesses reach it via InternalsVisibleTo; nothing else can.

member.summary: Record a user priority override. ★ Writes the STORE ONLY — it deliberately does NOT re-sort the live chain. member.name: M:AshForge.ModLoader.WorldStateBroker.ResetOverrides(AshForge.ModLoader.CapabilityId)
member.summary:
Clear every user override for a capability ("reset to declared order").
★ Reset is SPLIT exactly the way setting one is, because it is the inverse of setting one: the ENABLED half is undone live (every provider is re-enabled, then we re-resolve), while the PRIORITY half only takes effect at the next load — priority was bound at registration, and re-sorting now would flip an exclusive winner mid-tick under a consumer that already read the old value this tick. Clearing the store without re-enabling (the original behaviour) left a user-disabled provider disabled for the rest of the session while the store claimed it wasn't — the panel and reality disagreeing.

The runtime invokes StartupHook.Initialize() — a top-level type with no namespace and this exact signature — before the game's Main runs, when the env var DOTNET_STARTUP_HOOKS points at this assembly.
